newsitem.title: CHINA: FOCUS - China stocks charge ahead on foreign buying.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - China stocks charge ahead on foreign buying.

text.p: Foreign and Hong Kong investors flooded into China's stock markets on Thursday, sending Shenzhen's hard currency B share index up 10 percent and Shanghai's up by 9.9 percent, brokers said.
Further gains were in the cards as the B shares still look relatively cheap compared with China plays in Hong Kong, they said.
B shares rode a wave of liquidity from Hong Kong and outside of China to end higher with nearly all B shares in Shenzhen and Shanghai ending at their 10 percent daily limit up levels, brokers said.
"This is a historic moment for the B share market when just about every issue hit its limit-up level," said Cheng Li, an analyst at China Guotai Securities in Shenzhen.
Shenzhen's hard currency index leapt 13.78 points to its 10 percent limit-up level of 151.22 while turnover more than doubled to HK$266 million from Wednesday's HK$103 million.

Shanghai's B index closed the day up 7.227 points or 9.86 percent -- near the 10 percent daily limit up -- to 80.496 points on strong turnover of $23.748 million, compared with $15.267 million on Wednesday.
"Liquidity from foreign investors has entered the market," said an analyst at an Asian securities firm in Shanghai. "H shares have been so good that B shares have taken their turn."
H shares, shares of Chinese enterprises listed in Hong Kong, have recently registered meteoric rises.
Rumours that China would allow the establishment of joint investment funds between foreign and Chinese institutions to trade in B shares also supported the rise, analysts said.
Such funds would give domestic investors an indirect way to buy foreign currency B shares, which are technically reserved for foreigners, by investing in the funds, they said.

Officials at both the Shenzhen and Shanghai stock exchanges denied the rumours, but analysts said the government has hinted it would like to promote investment funds and joint venture mutual funds in China.
Although Shenzhen B shares ended mainly up at their 10 percent ceiling imposed by the government to narrow price movements, some recently-listed stocks shone on heavy trading volumes.

The heavily capitalised Bengang Steel Plates Co Ltd was the most actively traded stock with 24.4 million shares changing hands. Its shares, which closed at HK$2.59, shot through the HK$2.38 issue price.
The Shanghai B share index closed up 7.227 points or 9.86 percent higher.
Of Shanghai's 47 B shares, all gained on Thursday with most hitting their daily limit up of 10 percent.
Building machinery maker Shanghai Jintai Co was the top B share gainer, roaring ahead $0.012 or 10.17 percent to $0.130.

China's B shares had shed about 30 percent in the three months since Beijing clamped down in mid-May to end on what it saw as excessive stock speculation, while share prices in Hong Kong have been charging higher, analysts said.

Shenzhen's domestic currency A share index also gained on Thursday but with less gusto, rising 11.15 points, or 3.01 percent, to 382.01 on turnover of 3.4 billion yuan, compared with 3.2 billion on Wednesday.
The Shanghai A index closed up 48.325 points or 4.13 percent to 1,218.933 points on turnover of 3.402 billion yuan against 3.083 billion on Wednesday.
Shanghai's SSE30 blue chip rose 163.878 points or 4.68 percent to 3,665.727 points.
